name: Bonan
confidence_why: Li Hao's 2022 grammar of Gansu Bonan, Nugteren's 2011 Qinghai-Gansu Mongolic phonology and Li's 1986 article all put main stress on the final syllable of native words (moving onto the last suffix), and the only tension is Li 1986's claim that Linxia Chinese loans carry lexically fixed high pitch and the language is drifting toward tone, which Nugteren 2011 treats as loanword exceptions and Li Hao 2022 does not support, describing the accent as predictable and non-distinctive.

new_statements.quote: p.175: "The main stress of an indigenous Baonan word falls on the final syllable, i.e. if a morpheme appears in its root form, the stress falls on the final syllable of the root; if a morpheme occurs with suffixes, the stress falls on the last suffix. e.g. Habíb, Habib-né 'Habib-accusative case'. This stress placement rule, however, does not apply to the loan words from Linxia." ... "Stress in Baonan is characterized by high pitch and great acoustic energy." p.177: "The most significant result of the massive infusion of Linxia loan words into Baonan is that the one word-one stress rule is no longer valid. Instead of stress, what we have now is a contrast between high and low pitch on the syllables within a word."
new_statements.citation: Li, Charles N. 1986. The rise and fall of tones through diffusion. Proceedings of the Twelfth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 12).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's final-stress rule for the native stratum (root-final; last suffix when suffixed), and refines it with the phonetic correlates (high pitch + intensity) and a large class of exceptions: Linxia Chinese loans keep lexically fixed high pitch wherever the Chinese tone was non-low, so within the loan stratum placement is unpredictable and the author argues the system is drifting toward tone. He does not claim Bonan IS tonal, so the catalog's fixed: final syllable type is not overturned, but the data are from one Gansu (Linxia County) speaker in the 1980s.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In native (indigenous) Baonan vocabulary a single main stress falls on the last syllable of the word: on the root-final syllable of a bare root, and on the last suffix when suffixes are added (stress is realized as high pitch plus intensity). Loanwords from Linxia Chinese (40% of the author's 2,500-morpheme lexicon) do not obey this rule: their high pitch sits on whatever syllable had a Linxia 44/42/24 tone (low 22 syllables stay low), high pitch may fall on any or all syllables of a two- or three-syllable loan, the placement is lexically unpredictable, and it stays put when Baonan suffixes are added (p.179, 'Habib fajyn-go-dgi'). The author concludes the language is 'in the process of developing a tonal system', but explicitly leaves 'Is Baonan a tone language?' unanswered (p.179).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Loans may carry high pitch on more than one syllable (p.177: bisyllabic words 'with high pitch on both syllables, or on either one of the two syllables').
new_statements.exceptions: All Linxia Chinese loanwords (stress rule 'does not apply'); minimal pairs by pitch among loans, e.g. /xóxo/ 'box' vs /xoxó/ 'hairlip', /ʂídzɿ/ 'persimmon' vs /ʂɿdzí/ 'lion' (Table 3, p.177); the loan pitch overrides the final-stress rule even when Baonan suffixes are attached (p.179).
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1986 describes the Gansu (Linxia County, Muslim) dialect of Baonan from a single consultant, 'Habib', explicitly contrasting it with the Tongren (Qinghai) Lama-Buddhist dialect (p.173). Nugteren 2011 treats both branches: the example dialect for final accent is Ñantoq (Tongren, Qinghai) Baoan, the compound exceptions are labelled BaoÑ, and the Chinese-loan note refers to Ganhetan (Dahejia/Jishishan, Gansu) Baoan; his 'all QG languages' statement covers Bonan as a whole. Both works are about bona1250, not another language.

new_statements.quote: p.35: "Word-final accent is shared by all QG languages. This feature is also found in Moghol. [...] There are exceptions in the QG languages. In Eastern Yugur some word structures trigger changes in the position of the accent. In Baoan most exceptions involve compounds, which apparently carried the main accent on the last syllable of the first member, e.g. BaoÑ ˈnudə 'today' < *ene üdür 'this day', taˈwaraŋ '50' < *tabun harban 'five tens', ˈdebgə- 'to blink' < Amdo hdeb + *ki-." p.63: "In the Shirongol languages the accent normally falls on the last syllable." p.174: "In Ñantoq Baoan final accent is also the norm, e.g. mɵ'rə < *morïn 'horse'."
new_statements.citation: Nugteren, Hans (2011). Mongolic Phonology and the Qinghai-Gansu Languages. Rijksuniversiteit te Leiden. 563 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (final), stated for all QG languages and specifically for Ñantoq (Tongren, Qinghai) Baoan with a Baoan compound-exception list and a Ganhetan (Gansu) Baoan loanword note; adds the diachronic frame (possibly a shift from original first-syllable accent under Turkic/Iranian contact, unproven) and the corollary reduction of unaccented vowels.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bonan, like every Qinghai-Gansu Mongolic language (Shirongol group) and Moghol, places word accent on the last syllable; unaccented (especially first and medial) vowels reduce or drop as a corollary. Exceptions in Baoan are mainly old compounds that kept the accent on the last syllable of their first member (ˈnudə 'today', taˈwaraŋ '50'); the QG languages also show non-final accent in Arabic loans (ˈsaχari, ˈaġili) and in Chinese loans, where the non-final accent 'perhaps' reflects attempts to render tonal differences and avoid homophony (Dgx ʂïˈʒï 'lion' vs ˈʂïʒï 'persimmon', and the same opposition 'resolved in the same way in Ganhetan Baoan', fn. 13, p.35).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; compounds keep the main accent on the last syllable of the first member (p.35).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds (BaoÑ ˈnudə 'today', taˈwaraŋ '50', ˈdebgə- 'to blink'); Arabic loanwords with non-final accent; Chinese loanwords with non-final accent to preserve tonal distinctions (lion/persimmon pair in Dongxiang and Ganhetan Baoan, fn. 13); Eastern Yugur (not Baoan) has vowel-quality-driven deviations (sec. 3.14.5).
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1986 describes the Gansu (Linxia County, Muslim) dialect of Baonan from a single consultant, 'Habib', explicitly contrasting it with the Tongren (Qinghai) Lama-Buddhist dialect (p.173). Nugteren 2011 treats both branches: the example dialect for final accent is Ñantoq (Tongren, Qinghai) Baoan, the compound exceptions are labelled BaoÑ, and the Chinese-loan note refers to Ganhetan (Dahejia/Jishishan, Gansu) Baoan; his 'all QG languages' statement covers Bonan as a whole. Both works are about bona1250, not another language.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: both works put the main accent of native Bonan words on the final syllable (root-final, or on the last suffix), matching the catalog. The tension is about the loan stratum. Li 1986 (one Linxia County speaker, 1980s) claims the 'one word-one stress rule is no longer valid' because Linxia Chinese loans carry lexically fixed, unpredictable high pitch that survives suffixation, and reads this as an incipient tone system (while leaving 'Is Baonan a tone language?' open); Nugteren 2011 records the same phenomenon more cautiously as loanword exceptions (non-final accent in Chinese loans 'perhaps' to keep tonal distinctions, lion/persimmon in Ganhetan Baoan) without any claim that the language is becoming tonal. Nugteren adds a native class of exceptions (compounds accented on the first member) that Li does not mention. A third source already held by the project from the earlier reading but not in this work list, Li Hao 2022 (INALCO thesis, Gansu Bao'an, sec. 2.1.7.1 p.57), states that accent is predictable, final, non-distinctive and shifts to added suffixes, i.e. it does not support Li 1986's incipient-tone reading for the Gansu dialect a generation later.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: verbatim in the Nugteren 2011 text we hold (held under dong1285/src, not linked to this record), sec 1.5.1.1 p.35; sec 2.4.3 p.63 supports it. (2) Deciding source is a 2011 comparative-historical LOT dissertation summarising the QG group, not a primary description of Bonan; Glottolog lists two modern reference grammars (Fried 2010, 348 pp, Tongren; Li Hao 2022, 326 pp, Gansu) that outrank it for this language. (3) Li Hao 2022 downloaded from HAL: sec 2.1.7.1 p.57 states final-syllable accent (higher pitch, greater intensity, longer), predictable and non-distinctive, shifting onto suffixes; longer compounds keep per-lexeme accent; Mandarin loans carry contrastive pitch accents. This confirms 'fixed-dominant' final (final stress, not in the strict set) and matches the compound/loan exceptions already in the record. SPP 58 (Chuluu 1994) downloaded, silent on placement.
